We are a passionate team of students interested in technology, AI, and innovation. We aim to collaborate and create impactful solutions through creativity, teamwork, and problem-solving.
summary:
Project name: OrbitNexus

OrbitNexus is a health-monitoring software prototype designed to help astronauts understand changes in their health during space missions. It brings physiological readings, activity recognition, stress estimation, and anomaly detection into a single dashboard, helping users review their health indicators and identify changes that may need attention.

Our approach combines machine learning with insights from NASA’s Human Research Program and exploration of NASA’s Open Science Data Repository. Public physiological and activity datasets support prototype development, while NASA resources provide context about the challenges of maintaining health in space.

OrbitNexus addresses the challenge by making health information easier to interpret and supporting informed self-assessment. This matters during long missions, when communication with Earth can be delayed and crews need greater independence. The prototype supports health awareness rather than providing a clinical diagnosis. Future development will focus on validation, reliable wearable integration, and clear guidance for crew follow-up.
details:
Project Overview

OrbitNexus is a health-monitoring software prototype designed to help astronauts understand changes in their health during space missions. It brings physiological readings and machine-learning outputs into a single dashboard, helping users review their condition and identify changes that may require attention.

The project addresses a central question: when an astronaut’s readings change, how can the crew understand those changes and decide what to check next?

How It Works

The prototype receives physiological and activity inputs through its telemetry pipeline. A simulator supports demonstrations when physical sensors are unavailable. Specialized machine-learning components process different types of information:

* Activity recognition provides context about the user’s movement.

* Pulse-signal analysis estimates heart rate.

* Stress estimation explores patterns in physiological signals.

* Anomaly detection flags unusual combinations of readings for further review.

The dashboard presents these outputs together so users can interpret them in context. A conversational assistant, connected through Groq, provides an additional way to explore health information. This cloud-connected component requires internet access and is separate from the locally executed analysis components.

Scientific Foundation and Data

NASA Human Research Program resources informed our understanding of spaceflight hazards and the need for crew health monitoring. Public datasets, including BIDMC, PAMAP2, and WESAD, support the development of physiological-signal processing, activity recognition, and stress-estimation components.

NASA OSDR data also informed our exploration of spaceflight biology. Biological research data and wearable measurements serve different purposes in the project. They are not combined as if they were measurements from the same person, and gene-expression results are not treated as a real-time diagnosis of an astronaut.

Tools and Development

The prototype uses Python and a Flask backend with a browser-based dashboard and API endpoints. Its machine-learning components include Random Forest, ExtraTrees, XGBoost, and Isolation Forest. The project also explores incremental learning with an SGDClassifier to investigate how models could adapt as new observations become available.

Software testing focuses on API behavior, data flow, and integration between components. These checks establish software functionality, not clinical accuracy.

Creativity and Intended Impact

OrbitNexus combines activity context, physiological signals, and anomaly detection in one interface. Its creative contribution is connecting different indicators into a health-monitoring workflow that helps the user understand what has changed, rather than viewing each reading in isolation.

The intended impact is to support crew health awareness and informed self-assessment during long missions. Similar approaches could eventually support people in remote environments on Earth, subject to further validation.

Design Considerations and Limitations

We considered readability, individual differences, sensor quality, false alarms, connectivity limitations, and the distinction between simulated and measured data. Earth-based datasets do not establish performance in microgravity, and stress estimates are not mental-health diagnoses.

OrbitNexus is a research prototype, not a clinically validated medical device or a replacement for flight surgeons. Further work includes independent model evaluation, testing with representative mission data, verified wearable integration, privacy safeguards, and expert review of any health guidance.
